discovery: Optical lattice atomic clocks reaching 10^-18 precision and their use as probes of fundamental physics

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

motivation: Hidetoshi Katori conceived the optical lattice clock, trapping neutral atoms at a 'magic wavelength' where the lattice light leaves the clock transition unperturbed, and realised it experimentally with strontium. Jun Ye developed the strontium lattice clock into the most precise measuring instrument ever built, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, resolving the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample and controlling many-body interactions in the clock ensemble. Together they turned a novel idea in atomic spectroscopy into a new standard of precision. These clocks are now driving the redefinition of the SI second, enable relativistic geodesy with transportable instruments, and set stringent limits on variations of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark matter. This is a decisive experimental advance in atomic physics whose impact reaches far into metrology, geophysics and fundamental physics, and it is ripe for recognition.
